decisions.claim: B likes brains that make them think
decisions.reason: Turn 3 uses a tag question ('don't you?') which presupposes that B likes 'brains that make you think.' This is a direct presupposition from the speaker's own utterance.

decisions.claim: B has a country of origin
decisions.reason: Turn 17 uses the definite possessive 'your country,' which presupposes B has a country. This is a standard existential presupposition from a definite possessive.

decisions.claim: B likes games that make them think / intellectually challenging games
decisions.reason: c3 is a contextual reinterpretation of c1's 'brains that make you think' as 'intellectually challenging games.' Both derive from the same presupposition in Turn 3 and refer to the same property of B. c1 is the more literal and grounded statement.

decisions.claim: B is from a country where mah-jong is culturally prominent
decisions.reason: Turn 17 says 'I thought everyone in your country were experts at mah-jong!' The phrase 'I thought' signals A's prior assumption, which A then corrects or questions. This does not establish that B's country is where mah-jong is culturally prominent; it only establishes B has a country (c2). A's mistaken belief about mah-jong expertise does not transfer to B as a fact about their country.
decisions.counterexample: B could be from a country where mah-jong is not prominent at all, and A's assumption was simply wrong.

design: dual route, targeted rescue, globally grouped evidence adjudication
